scenarios.name: single, retirement income below the $31,110 cap (KY's exclusion carries no age gate, so this and the next case vary income, not age)
scenarios.source: Kentucky Revised Statutes 141.019(1)(g)1.b (current codified text, https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=57914, effective 07/15/2026): 'For taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2018, exclude up to thirty-one thousand one hundred ten dollars ($31,110) of total distributions from pension plans, annuity contracts, profit-sharing plans, retirement plans, or employee savings plans.' The 2026 amendments to this statute (2026 Ky. Acts ch. 161 sec. 7 and ch. 198 sec. 48, both effective 07/15/2026) touch subsections (r), (j), (k), (l), (m) -- R&D expensing, mortgage interest, tips, overtime, and vehicle-loan interest -- and do not change (g)1.b, so $31,110 stands for TY2026. HB 146 (25RS, introduced 01/08/25, Bill Request 822, 'AN ACT relating to the taxation of retirement distributions') proposed raising this to $41,110; its last recorded action per the General Assembly's own bill-history page (https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/25rs/hb146.html) is '02/04/25: to Appropriations & Revenue (H)' with no further action recorded through the end of the 2025 session, so it died in committee and was never enacted. The statute carries no age qualifier at all -- unlike Colorado, Georgia, and most other states' retirement exclusions, KRS 141.019(1)(g) applies at any age. Single filer, pension income $25,000, all of it under the cap: Schedule P (2025, form 42A740-P (10-25), https://revenue.ky.gov/Forms/Schedule%20P%20(2025).pdf) Part III Line 3 'Enter the lesser of line 2 or $31,110' = 25000, fully excluded. Kentucky AGI = 25000-25000 = 0. Form 740 Line 10 nonitemizer standard deduction for 2026 is $3,360 (Kentucky DOR, 'Kentucky DOR Announces 2026 Standard Deduction', https://revenue.ky.gov/News/Pages/Kentucky-DOR-Announces-2026-Standard-Deduction.aspx: 'the standard deduction for 2026 is $3,360, an increase of $90.'). Taxable income = max(0, 0-3360) = 0. Tax = $0.

scenarios.name: single, retirement income above the $31,110 cap: excess is taxed at the 2026 flat 3.5% rate
scenarios.source: Same statute and cap as above; single filer, pension income $50,000. Schedule P Line 3 = lesser of 50000 or 31110 = 31110 excluded. Kentucky AGI = 50000-31110 = 18890. Standard deduction $3,360 (Kentucky DOR, 'Kentucky DOR Announces 2026 Standard Deduction', https://revenue.ky.gov/News/Pages/Kentucky-DOR-Announces-2026-Standard-Deduction.aspx: 'the standard deduction for 2026 is $3,360, an increase of $90.'). Taxable income = 18890-3360 = 15530. Kentucky's flat rate for tax years beginning on or after 1/1/2026 is 3.5%, per the DOR's own 2026 withholding formula ('2026 Kentucky Tax Rate: 3.5% of taxable income'), which implements House Bill 1 (2025 RS), signed by Governor Beshear, amending the individual income tax rate from 4% to 3.5% effective January 1, 2026. Tax = 15530*0.035 = $543.55.

scenarios.name: MFJ, both spouses have their own qualifying retirement income: Schedule P computes and combines each spouse's own $31,110 exclusion, it is not one household cap
scenarios.source: Schedule P (2025, form 42A740-P (10-25)), page 2, 'LINE-BY-LINE INSTRUCTIONS', 'Column A, Column B': 'This exclusion is for each taxpayer. A taxpayer and spouse must compute and claim their own exclusion, regardless of filing status.' Page 1 explicitly instructs 'Joint filers -- Combine lines 4(a) and 4(b) and enter on appropriate form', i.e. compute Column A (spouse) and Column B (yourself) separately on Schedule P and then ADD them before the single combined figure ever reaches Schedule M line 9 / Form 740 line 8 (Form 740 (2025), https://revenue.ky.gov/Forms/740%20(2025).pdf, filing status 3, 'Married, filing joint return', reports combined income and deductions in Column B only -- confirmed by Form 740 page 1's Column B header 'Yourself (or Joint)', so joint filers do use a single combined AGI/deduction column for everything EXCEPT this per-spouse Schedule P computation). Primary (age 66) has $35,000 of own pension income: min(35000,31110)=31110. Spouse (age 64) has $35,000 of own pension income: min(35000,31110)=31110. Combined exclusion = 31110+31110 = 62220. Kentucky AGI = 70000-62220 = 7780. Standard deduction (joint, one combined $3,360) : taxable income = 7780-3360 = 4420. Tax = 4420*0.035 = $154.70. StateTaxData.swift's KY config sets no exemptionAppliesPerIndividual override (defaults false) and no exemptionAttribution override (defaults household), so the engine pools both spouses' pension income into ONE $31,110 cap instead of two, which will materially overtax this household -- this is a per-individual attribution gap the 2026-08-02 audit's 'Kentucky -- $31,110 stands' finding did not examine (it checked only the dollar figure against HB 146, not MFJ attribution).

knownDefect.summary: KY's config has no exemptionAppliesPerIndividual/exemptionAttribution override so the engine pools both spouses' pension income and applies ONE $31,110 household cap, when Schedule P computes each spouse's own $31,110 exclusion separately (Columns A and B) and combines them regardless of filing status.

scenarios.name: MFJ, only primary spouse has retirement income: single-pool cap and per-spouse cap agree, no defect
scenarios.source: Same Schedule P mechanics as above, but only the primary (age 66) has $40,000 of pension income; the spouse (age 58, still working) has $30,000 of unrelated wage income and no pension of her own. Primary Schedule P Column B: min(40000,31110)=31110. Spouse Column A: $0 (no pension income to enter). Combined exclusion = 31110, identical to what a single pooled cap would also produce since only one spouse contributes to the pool. Kentucky AGI = 70000-31110 = 38890. Standard deduction (joint) = 3360. Taxable income = 38890-3360 = 35530. Tax = 35530*0.035 = $1,243.55. Contrast case: the per-individual attribution gap above only bites when BOTH spouses actually have their own qualifying retirement distributions.
